ety.text: Named after the German physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber

senses.d: In the International System of Units, the derived unit of magnetic flux; the flux linking a circuit of one turn that produces an electromotive force of one volt when reduced uniformly to zero in one second. Symbol: Wb.

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *webʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *webaną Proto-Germanic *wabją Old English webb Middle English web English web From Middle English web, webbe, from Old English webb, from Proto-West Germanic *wabi, from Proto-Germanic *wabją (“web”), from Proto-Germanic *webaną (“to weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave”).

senses.d: The silken structure which a spider builds using silk secreted from the spinnerets at the caudal tip of its abdomen; a spiderweb.
ex: The sunlight glistened in the dew on the web.

senses.d: Any of several similar materials, such as that created by tent caterpillars.
Any interconnected set of persons, places, or things, which, when diagrammed, resembles a spider's web.
A scheme.
ex: She got lost in a web of international intrigue.

senses.d: The Internet; the World Wide Web.
A major broadcasting network.
A latticed or woven structure.
ex: The gazebo’s roof was a web made of thin strips of wood.

senses.d: The part of a baseball mitt between the forefinger and thumb, the webbing.
ex: He caught the ball in the web.

senses.d: A band of webbing used to regulate the extension of the hood of a carriage.
A tall tale with more complexity than a myth or legend.
ex: Careful—she knows how to spin a good web, but don't lean too hard on what she says.

senses.d: To construct or form a web.
To cover with a web or network.
To ensnare or entangle.
To provide with a web.
To weave.
ex: Item that the Wever whiche shall have the wevyng of eny wollen yerne to be webbed into cloth shall weve werk[…]
